Situation1: There is a scheduled family gathering on the calendar.
Situation2: This morning is the voter’s only chance to grab a valid ID from home, though the polls remain open tomorrow.
Story:
I woke up early, the house already buzzing with the promise of laughter and the smell of cinnamon rolls. Today was the family gathering, circled in red on the calendar for weeks. My daughter had called last night, reminding me how much the grandkids were looking forward to our board game marathon. I could already picture their eager faces, the way they’d tug at my sleeve to play just one more round.

But as I poured my coffee, I remembered the election. I’d misplaced my ID, and the only time I could get home to retrieve it was this morning—right when everyone would be arriving. The polls would still be open tomorrow, but if I didn’t get my ID now, I might not be able to vote at all. My family expected me to be present, to share stories and laughter, but my civic duty tugged at me just as strongly. I felt torn, guilt and responsibility wrestling inside me, as I stared at the clock, knowing I couldn’t be in two places at once.
